memoryText: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read 1 Peter 1:3-4 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Peter begins with praise, not with instruction. Before he tells his readers what to do, he reminds them what God has done. Everything flows from mercy: “According to his great mercy, he has caused us to be born again.” We did not earn it, and we did not start it.

The hope is “living” because it is tied to the resurrection of Jesus Christ. A dead Savior would give a dead hope. Because he lives, our hope is not wishful thinking but a confident expectation.

The inheritance has three descriptions: imperishable (it cannot decay), undefiled (it cannot be corrupted), unfading (it cannot lose its beauty). And it is kept in heaven for you. Nothing here is stored where thieves or time can reach it.

When your week was hard, which phrase did you need most? Say it back to God as a prayer of thanks.
weekInReview: This week you read James 3 to 5 and the opening of 1 Peter. James showed us the tongue that no human can tame, the two kinds of wisdom, the source of quarrels in our desires, humility before God, the brevity of life, the warning to the rich, patience until the Lord comes, and prayer for the sick and for the wanderer. Three psalms offered further wisdom: Psalm 12 on lying lips and the pure words of the LORD, Psalm 15 on who may dwell in God’s tent, and Psalm 24 on the clean hands that ascend the hill and the King of glory who enters the gates. In 1 Peter 1:1 to 2:12, we heard of a living hope, tested faith, a call to holiness, redemption by the precious blood of Christ, and our identity as a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, and people for God’s own possession.
reflectionQuestions: James says no human being can tame the tongue. Where has your speech been most difficult to control, and how can you ask God to change your heart so that your words follow?
Psalms 15 and 24 describe someone with clean hands and a pure heart. Since none of us fits this description, how does Christ’s perfect righteousness change the way you approach God?
Peter calls believers “a people for his own possession” who were “once not a people.” How does belonging to God’s people shape the way you live as an exile in this world?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for rest and for the living hope in Jesus.
Ask him to guard your faith.
